content: Catheter-associated infections are a significant concern in healthcare settings. Therefore, it is essential to conduct further research on the safe insertion, maintenance, access, and removal of intravascular catheters across diverse healthcare environments. Following extensive discussions, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified several critical areas for research to enhance the safety and practicality of using peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs), peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs), and midline vascular catheters (MCVs) globally. Identified Research Gaps: 1. Insertion Techniques: Investigating cost-effective alternatives to sterile barrier precautions for PICC and peripheral arterial catheter (PAC) insertion in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Evaluating adherence to aseptic no-touch techniques for PIVC insertion in various clinical settings to identify high-risk scenarios requiring special considerations. Determining the optimal size of drapes and the necessity of clinicians wearing masks during PIVC insertion. Assessing the benefits and drawbacks of aseptic no-touch techniques for PIVC insertion. 2. Skin Disinfection: Standardizing comparator products in studies evaluating chlorhexidine-containing skin disinfectants to better assess their effectiveness. Investigating the benefits and harms of chlorhexidine-containing dressings for both PICCs and PIVCs. 3. Training and Competency: Identifying the most efficient methods for catheter insertion training, particularly in resource-limited settings. Researching strategies to maintain catheter insertion competency over time. 4. Glove Use: Exploring cost-effective materials for single-use gloves that maximize tactile agility and minimize allergy risks for healthcare workers. Developing affordable sterile gloves with good tactile features to address cost and equity concerns in LMICs. Evaluating the impact of glove-wearing on catheter insertion success rates and infection risks. 5. Catheter Insertion Kits: Designing standardized PIVC insertion kits suitable for diverse healthcare settings to improve cost-effectiveness and availability, especially in LMICs. 6. Ultrasound-Guided Insertion: Researching optimal teaching methods for ultrasound use during catheter insertion, including standardized cleaning protocols. 7. Insertion Sites: Identifying the best distal arm sites for PIVC insertion based on patient factors such as pain, mobility, and risk of phlebitis. Investigating clinical scenarios where lower limb PIVC insertion is necessary to inform the development of alternative venous access devices. 8. Catheter Dressings: Determining the optimal occlusive semi-permeable dressing for use in all climates, particularly in LMICs. Evaluating whether sterile dressings are routinely required for PIVCs. 9. Insertion Teams: Assessing the cost-benefit of using formal PIVC insertion teams to reduce complications and improve patient outcomes. 10. Local Anesthetics: Identifying the best topical local anesthetics for catheter insertion in terms of absorption and drying time to enhance feasibility in emergencies. Investigating patient-related issues, such as pain and discomfort, associated with local anesthetic use. 11. Catheter Maintenance: Determining the optimal methods for catheter maintenance using intermittent infusion and the ideal type of infusion fluid. Comparing the risks and benefits of saline versus anticoagulant solutions for lock-off flushing of PIVCs and PICCs. 12. Catheter Removal: Conducting trials to define the optimal time for scheduled PIVC removal and the safety of clinically indicated removal. Investigating the impact of scheduled versus clinically indicated PIVC changes on infection rates in LMICs. Researching the appropriate timing for removing or replacing PIVCs inserted under emergency conditions. 13. Catheter Selection: Identifying situations where multi-lumen PICCs are clinically required to aid resource planning and protocol development. Evaluating the complications associated with the vein-to-catheter diameter ratio rather than the number of PICC lumens. Comparing the advantages of multi-lumen PICCs versus multi-lumen central venous catheters. 14. Monitoring and Evaluation: Routine monitoring of complications associated with PIVCs and PICCs, correlating data with adherence to clinical guidelines. Investigating healthcare-associated bloodstream infections (BSIs) to determine their source and whether they are catheter-related. Dissemination and Implementation: The guidelines for preventing bloodstream infections and other catheter-associated infections are available in print and online. They will remain valid for five years, with updates based on emerging evidence. WHO plans to translate the guidelines into multiple languages and disseminate them through regional offices, the Global Infection Prevention and Control Network, and other channels. Evidence briefs targeting policymakers and program managers will also be developed to enhance guideline uptake. Conclusion: The outlined research priorities aim to address critical gaps in the prevention and management of catheter-associated infections. By focusing on these areas, healthcare systems worldwide can improve patient safety, reduce complications, and enhance the overall effectiveness of intravascular catheter use.
